description: Learn to throw HTTP exceptions and write custom global exception handlers for your API.

slides.title: The HTTPException
slides.content:
# Returning Errors 🚨

In a normal Python function, you `raise Exception()`. 
In FastAPI, if you raise a standard Exception, it crashes the route and returns a generic `500 Internal Server Error`.

To return a proper, helpful error to the client, you must raise an `HTTPException`.

```python_not
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: str):
    if item_id not in items_db:
        # Raise an HTTPException to stop the route immediately
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return {"item": items_db[item_id]}
```

slides.title: Custom Exception Handlers
slides.content:
# Global Error Catching 🧤

What if you have a custom exception in your business logic (e.g., `UserBannedException`), and you want FastAPI to automatically return a `403 Forbidden` every time it is raised *anywhere* in your app?

You can use the `@app.exception_handler()` decorator.

```python_not
from fastapi import Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

class UserBannedException(Exception):
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name

# Register the global handler
@app.exception_handler(UserBannedException)
async def banned_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: UserBannedException):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=403,
        content={"message": f"Oops! {exc.name} is banned."},
    )
```

slides.title: Raising the Custom Exception
slides.content:
# Clean Business Logic 🧹

Now, your route doesn't need to know anything about HTTP status codes!

```python_not
@app.get("/users/{username}")
async def get_user(username: str):
    if username == "hacker_bob":
        # Just raise your normal Python exception!
        raise UserBannedException(name=username)
        
    return {"user": username}
```
When `UserBannedException` is raised, FastAPI catches it globally and runs the `banned_exception_handler`, returning the proper JSON to the user.

slides.title: Knowledge Check: Exceptions
slides.quizQuestion: Why should you raise an `HTTPException` instead of a standard Python `ValueError` when an item is not found in the database?
quizOptions: Because HTTPException allows you to specify the exact HTTP status code (e.g., 404) and a detail message to send to the client.
Because standard Exceptions do not work in asynchronous functions.
To prevent the Pydantic validator from crashing.

slides.title: Overriding RequestValidationError
slides.content:
# Customizing Validation Errors 💅

When Pydantic validation fails, FastAPI automatically throws a `RequestValidationError` and returns a `422 Unprocessable Entity`.

If you don't like the default format of the 422 error, you can override it globally!

```python_not
from fastapi.exceptions import RequestValidationError

@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    # 'exc.errors()' contains the list of Pydantic validation errors
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=400, # Changing the default 422 to a 400
        content={"message": "You sent bad data!", "details": exc.errors()},
    )
```

slides.title: Handling 500 Errors
slides.content:
# Catching Everything Else 🕸️

Sometimes, your code just crashes. A variable is None, or a list index is out of bounds.
This causes an unhandled Exception, resulting in a `500 Internal Server Error`.

You can add a global "catch-all" handler to log these errors or return a friendly message.

```python_not
@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def global_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    # Log the error to your monitoring system (Sentry, Datadog, etc.)
    print(f"CRITICAL ERROR: {exc}")
    
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=500,
        content={"message": "Our servers are currently on fire. Please try again later."},
    )
```

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Summary 🎉

You know how to gracefully handle failure!

## Key Takeaways
- ✅ **HTTPException:** Use this to intentionally stop a request and return a specific HTTP status code (like 404 Not Found or 401 Unauthorized).
- ✅ **Custom Handlers:** Use `@app.exception_handler()` to map standard Python exceptions to specific HTTP responses globally.
- ✅ **RequestValidationError:** Override this specific exception if you want to change the format of Pydantic's default 422 validation errors.
- ✅ **Catch-All Handler:** You can create a global handler for `Exception` to gracefully handle server crashes and log them to your monitoring tools.
